title: 21 families cleared off two sewage plant sites in Muntinlupa, and nine renting families moved off a third parcel
place: Barangay Tunasan and Barangay Cupang, Muntinlupa City, Metro Manila, Philippines

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Project P113844, Metro Manila Wastewater Management Project, loan IBRD 81620-PH of US$275 million to the Land Bank of the Philippines with the guarantee of the Republic of the Philippines, on-lent to the two Metro Manila water concessionaires. The completion report of 23 December 2020 gives approval on 15 May 2012, effectiveness on 19 October 2012, a mid-term review on 30 January 2014, an original closing date of 30 June 2017 and actual closing on 30 June 2020, after closing-date extensions on 14 June 2017 and 27 June 2019. All US$275 million was disbursed; the borrower’s own contribution was US$142,114,000 against US$96.7 million at appraisal and a revised US$228 million, and total project cost was US$417,114,000 against US$371.7 million at appraisal. The project was classified Financial Intermediary Assessment (F) for environmental purposes. The completion report says the project triggered Environmental Assessment (OP 4.01) and Natural Habitats (OP 4.04), at paragraph 68, and the involuntary resettlement policy OP 4.12, at paragraph 71, and rates both environmental and social safeguards Satisfactory. The Evaluation Group’s review gives the same three, citing those two paragraphs; the appraisal document’s checkbox table of triggered policies does not survive in the Bank’s text version of that document. The report rates the outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory and monitoring Substantial; the Evaluation Group's review, filed under 17 November 2021 and carrying no date on its own face, agrees on outcome and monitoring but rates Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, giving as its reason "There were shortcomings in project design." The Muntinlupa subprojects were the Cupang plant (US$27.68 million), the Tunasan plant (US$16.95 million plus US$4.94 million for nutrient removal) and the 4.12 km Muntinlupa conveyance system (US$14.74 million), all three unfinished at loan closing.

companies.name: Maynilad Water Services, Inc.
companies.role: Concessionaire for the west zone of the Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System and the proponent of the Tunasan and Cupang subprojects; it bought both plant sites and ran the resettlement, which the Bank’s documents describe as carried out under the project’s loan covenant. The two resettlement completion reports record the compensation for structures, the replacement plots and the transfer costs as paid by the selling landowners rather than by the concessionaire.

companies.name: Land Bank of the Philippines
companies.role: Borrower of the Bank loan and the financial intermediary that on-lent it to the concessionaires; a state-owned bank whose mandate is lending to farmers and fisherfolk.

companies.name: Dragonhart
companies.role: Contractor for the Muntinlupa sewerage conveyance system, named as such in the land acquisition completion report of May 2018, which records it working with Maynilad and the design consultant on a trenchless pipe-laying option to avoid moving the people living under the Pasong Diablo bridge.

community: Two of the project's sewage plant sites had people living on them. The Bank's completion report says all the land was bought from willing sellers, "including the lot needed for the Tunasan and Cupang STPs, which necessitated the physical displacement of informal settler families", and that the procedures were complied with "including in the relocation of 21 informal settler families in Tunasan STP and in Cupang STP". Its footnote 28 splits that figure: Tunasan 14, Cupang 7. At Tunasan, the resettlement completion report of 8 March 2017 names the 14 households and says their structures were cleared after compensation was agreed and paid. They had no claim on the land: the report quotes the project's own entitlement matrix, "Affected squatters and other informal settlers will not be entitled to compensation for affected land but will be compensated for affected structures and other investments made on the land and relocation assistance." The replacement plots were sold to them, not given: the sellers’ attorney-in-fact parcelled a 2,999.67 square metre lot into 32 square metre plots at 2,000 pesos a square metre, the zonal value, 64,000 pesos a plot, to be paid off over ten years after two rent-free years, at 500 pesos a month for a 32 square metre plot and 1,000 pesos for 64 square metres, with no interest. The report sets out what the landowner gave up and treats it as part of the package: 15,900 pesos a household in transfer and title costs, 16,000 pesos in free use of the land for two years, and 50,614 pesos in forgone interest over the ten years, which it adds to 82,514 pesos a household. The 14 were moved as a group to a site within walking distance of the old one, and the report says the move “would cause no significant socio-economic disruptions or physical adjustments to their usual activities”. Each household also got between 10,000 and 20,000 pesos from the landowner for its house, depending on the structure, 160,000 pesos in all paid on 17 May 2013; physical transfer help worth at least 5,000 pesos in kind rather than cash; and labour to pull their houses down so they could keep the materials. Ten of the 14 were living on the new lot by June 2016; four were not, and the report names them: one family went back to Palawan, one rents near his work in Muntinlupa, one lives with his parents, and one is in Canada and passed his plot to his brother. A Bank due-diligence visit on 20 June 2014 found four things unresolved at the new site: water connections, electricity, safe access in place of a narrow easement, and copies of land titles. An updated plan of 10 November 2014 was published to cover the restoration of those utilities, and the resettlement completion report of 8 March 2017 says it follows the resolution of those measures. It also says that most of the displaced people it interviewed signified contentment with what they received. At Cupang, the resettlement completion report of 28 May 2014 says eight informal-settler households, 44 people, were displaced from the Arevalo-Cruz Estate, which Maynilad bought from seven siblings. Seven of the eight were paid 143,000 pesos between them for the shanties that were removed and signed affidavits of willingness to vacate; the eighth was not moved off the land: Marjorie Solomon’s father, a transient occupant, was sick and could not move, so the landowner paid to rebuild the family’s shanty on the part of the estate that was not sold, less than ten metres from where it stood, and gave 5,000 pesos for the transition. They had been given a notice to vacate by the landowner dated 14 October 2010 and 90 days to take their structures down. On a second parcel bought for the same plant, Elenita Daco’s, a six-door two-storey apartment block and a bungalow were taken down to open access to the plant from Manuel L. Quezon Road, and the families renting them moved out. The report counts them twice and differently: its Table 3 names nine heads of household with 47 household members between them, while its own summary paragraph says “The fifteen (15) households (7 informal settlers and 8 renters) of the properties except for 2 ... left the area after receiving payments from the landowner.” Their rental contracts had expired in 2009 and were never renewed; they were given notice to vacate from September 2012, signed affidavits of willingness to move, and all had gone by January 2013, with more than three months’ notice, a month’s rent each as transition help and the last month’s rent not collected. One of them, Susan Mendones, moved her sari-sari store less than 50 metres. Three years after that, on 25 April 2017, the news site Interaksyon reported that a house in Barangay Cupang collapsed at about three in the morning and two neighbouring houses were damaged, and that “Initial observations pointed to the possibility of ground subsidence as the sewerage project was removing soil nearby”. The same report gives rain as part of the cause: a resident said it had rained through the night, and the report says several days of rain “may have caused softening and mobility of the foundation soil”. It names a contractor of Maynilad, Dragon Health Corporation, as doing the digging, says the contractor assured residents it would shoulder the consequences, and reports that the barangay chairman halted the work for technical assessments. No Bank document mentions that collapse, and no document found says whether the excavation was part of the Bank-financed conveyance system. At loan closing the Bank listed, as social safeguards business still outstanding on that conveyance system, a memorandum of agreement to be concluded "with the owner of the house affected by the Bayanan Pumping Station in Cupang, Muntinlupa"; the same report's appendix describes the same house as one that "will be affected".
outcome: The loan closed on 30 June 2020 with the Cupang plant 91.99 per cent built, the Tunasan plant 91.57 per cent built and the Muntinlupa conveyance system 90.48 per cent built. The Bank left three social safeguards matters for Maynilad to settle after closing, with six-monthly reports: the construction method at a Valenzuela pumping station, the agreement with the owner of the house at the Bayanan pumping station in Cupang, and negotiations with the landowner on the Tunasan influent line, failing which the line would be re-routed to a steel bridge. The resettlement completion report says the Tunasan households' water and power were restored and titles prepared; no later document was found on the Bayanan house.

title: 35 families moved off irrigation canal land, and 19.7 hectares signed over by 299 project-affected people, on ten Philippine irrigation systems
place: Ten national irrigation systems, Philippines, with the resettlement sites in Region 5 (Bicol) and Region 11 (Davao), and the largest counted group of canal-easement households on the Tigman-Hinagyanan-Inarihan River Irrigation System in Camarines Sur

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Project P088926, Participatory Irrigation Development Project, loan 7709-PH (IBRD-77090). Loan agreement conformed 7 August 2009. The completion report of 25 April 2019 gives approval on 24 June 2009, effectiveness on 3 November 2009, a mid-term review on 10 May 2013, an original closing date of 31 March 2015 and actual closing on 31 August 2018, after four restructurings (11 February 2015, 24 September 2015, 31 March 2016 and 13 February 2017). The loan was US$70.36 million at approval, revised to US$58,015,957, all of which was disbursed; the borrower put in US$42,844,004, against US$43.23 million planned, and total project cost was US$100,859,961 against US$113.59 million planned. Environmental category: Partial Assessment (B). On safeguards the report says: "Overall, the NIS did not pose large-scale adverse social and environmental impacts, but pertinent safeguards policies were triggered, including Involuntary Resettlement (Operational Policy or OP 4.12), Indigenous Peoples (OP 4.10), Safety of Dams (OP 4.37), Environmental Assessment (OP 4.01), and Pest Management (OP 4.09)." The word "including" is the report's own, so this may not be the full list; the appraisal document's checkbox table does not survive in the Bank's text version of that document. The report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and the quality of monitoring Modest, and rates overall safeguards performance Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review, filed by the Bank under 21 June 2019 and carrying no date on its own face, agrees on outcome, Bank performance and monitoring, and rates the quality of the completion report Substantial.

companies.name: National Irrigation Administration
companies.role: Implementing agency. A government corporation attached to the Department of Agriculture that builds and runs the Philippines' national irrigation systems and collects irrigation service fees; its Right of Way Management and regional irrigation offices handled the land acquisition, and the project also paid for the staff reduction under its own Rationalization Plan.

community: The project rebuilt 58 national irrigation systems. Land had to be acquired on ten of them. The Bank's completion report counts 960 families: "a total of 960 families, consisting of 401 landowners, 288 informal settlers and 271 owners of crops trees that had encroached into existing canal right of way." Of the informal settlers, "35 families (13 are IPs) have availed of the resettlement sites that NIA and host Local Government Units (LGUs) have provided while the rest opted to relocate on their own or set back their homes from the canal after receiving cash compensation." The borrower’s own annex to the same report describes the same 960 as “960 PAPs whose properties and livelihood opportunities were affected by project construction”, the report’s acronym list defining PAP as project affected person, puts the resettlement sites in Region 5 and Region 11 and says 299 project-affected people handed over 197,767 square metres, about 19.7 hectares, of right of way by deed of donation. Of the 401 landowners, who lost an average of 708 square metres each, 102 took compensation at the prevailing market price and the rest donated their land. The report records "some initial delays in the payment of compensation due to lack of legal supporting documents from claimants and different documentary requirements for the various types of tenurial status", says these "were all settled", and says funds for three absentee claimants were put in a trust account. It says the feedback from landowners who donated was generally positive, and the borrower's annex says living conditions improved, especially for those moved to the resettlement sites. On one system, the Tigman-Hinagyanan-Inarihan River Irrigation System in Camarines Sur, the resettlement action plan of August 2008 counted 204 informal-settler households scattered inside the works area of seven irrigators’ associations on a system that runs through four municipalities of Camarines Sur, of whom 45 said they would vacate and wanted compensation, a project-provided relocation plot and transport help. No document found reports how many of those 204 were moved.
outcome: The project closed on 31 August 2018. The completion report of April 2019 and the Evaluation Group's review treat the resettlement as finished and rate safeguards performance Satisfactory. Neither document says what the 35 families were paid, where the resettlement sites are, or what became of the 204 households counted on the Camarines Sur system in 2008.

title: 397 families moved off the Rodriguez ecotourism site, some still waiting at project close
place: Rodriguez (Montalban), Rizal, Philippines, with the relocation site at Kasiglahan Village Phase 1-D, Barangay San Jose

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Project P070899. The completion report covers the original loan and the additional financing together and gives no project number for the additional financing; the number P117470 is the one ICIJ files it under. Loan 7205-PH (IBRD-72050) of US$5 million for the Laguna de Bay Institutional Strengthening and Community Participation Project, dated 26 January 2004, approved 4 December 2003, effective 2 April 2004; additional financing of US$10 million as loan 8035-PH (IBRD-80350), approved 12 April 2011, dated 12 May 2011, effective 27 July 2011, of which US$4.5 million was cancelled on 11 July 2013 and a further US$3 million at project closing. The closing date was extended five times: four extensions totalling 27 months, to 30 April 2011, and then a fifth of three years when the additional financing became effective, to 30 April 2014, when the project closed. The Bank's completion report of 25 November 2014 gives the amount disbursed as US$6.80 million on its data sheet and US$6.83 million in its financing table. Environmental category B. The involuntary resettlement policy OP 4.12 and the indigenous peoples policy were triggered. The report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory, the government's performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, and risk to the development outcome Substantial. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 8 October 2015 agrees on outcome, Bank performance and borrower performance, and prints the risk rating as Significant.

lenders.name: Netherlands Ministry of Foreign Affairs
lenders.role: Parallel grant TF-52826 of US$5 million at appraisal for the institutional development component, of which US$4.24 million was spent, per the completion report's financing table.

companies.name: Laguna Lake Development Authority
companies.role: Implementing agency, the national government corporation that regulates the Laguna de Bay basin; it lent project funds on to local governments, which chose and built the sub-projects.

companies.name: Municipal Government of Rodriguez, Rizal
companies.role: The local government that ran the ecotourism sub-project. The Bank's completion report says it had to relocate and resettle the 397 families and that it prepared the resettlement action plan, and that it is leading the building of the Sitio Sapo site with the National Housing Authority on land development.

community: The project lent money to local governments around Laguna de Bay for small environmental works. The Bank's completion report says one sub-project carried a relocation and resettlement requirement: "The Rodriquez LGU had to relocate and resettle 397 families of illegal settlers from their ecotourism sub-project site." Most of those families were accommodated at Kasiglahan Village Phase 1-D in Barangay San Jose. The relocation of a few families was still outstanding when the project closed, because the Sitio Sapo resettlement site had been held up over its development permit and environmental compliance certificate; the report says that site was still under construction, led by the municipality with the National Housing Authority on land development and a non-governmental organisation on social preparation and house building. The report also records one expropriation case filed over the road right of way for the Pangil materials recovery facility sub-project. The Rodriguez sub-projects appear under the additional financing in the report's own list of sub-projects. For the rest of the project the report says all land acquisition was done after securing the consent of the owners affected, through purchase, lease, donation, usufruct or exchange, and it rates compliance with the involuntary resettlement policy satisfactory. The ecotourism site also drew a claim from indigenous people that a religious ritual site of theirs lay inside it; the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples investigated, cleared the sub-project, and the municipality signed an agreement giving the indigenous group 3 per cent of the sub-project's revenue.
outcome: The project closed on 30 April 2014. The Evaluation Group's review of October 2015 lists the relocation of a few families to Sitio Sapo as one of two matters still pending at closure, the other being the Pangil expropriation case. Neither document says how many families were still waiting, and no later document was found that says whether the Sitio Sapo site was finished.

title: Two villages cleared for the Raciborz Dolny flood polder
place: Nieboczowy and Ligota Tworkowska, gmina Lubomia, Silesian Voivodeship, Poland

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Odra River Basin Flood Protection Project, P086768, loan IBRD-74360. Approved 21 March 2007, closed 30 June 2020 after a six-year extension. US$184 million committed and US$166.56 million disbursed, against a total project cost of US$1.019 billion; in euros the completion report gives 131.94 million disbursed of an original commitment of 140.1 million, about 91 per cent (completion report, 28 January 2021). The completion report rates the outcome Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 10 June 2021 also rates it Satisfactory.

lenders.name: European Commission
lenders.role: Co-financier through the EU Cohesion Fund. The completion report's cost-overrun table gives 340.56 million euros disbursed at closing against 130 million estimated at appraisal (completion report, 28 January 2021).

lenders.name: Council of Europe Development Bank
lenders.role: Co-financier. The completion report's cost-overrun table gives 204.66 million euros disbursed at closing against 204.9 million estimated at appraisal, and records that the Bank and the Development Bank ran joint project review missions (completion report, 28 January 2021).

companies.name: Regional Authority for Water Management in Gliwice (RZGW Gliwice)
companies.role: State water authority for the upper Odra basin, and the project implementation unit for the Raciborz dry polder and for the resettlement. It later became part of PGW WP, the State Water Holding Polish Waters. The completion report names no construction contractor.

companies.name: Lower Silesian Board for Amelioration and Hydraulic Structures (DZMiUW)
companies.role: The regional water-engineering board for Lower Silesia. The completion report of 28 January 2021 records that the project coordination unit monitored the construction of the new village of Nieboczowy and the process of land acquisition by this board; the report does not say which works that land acquisition was for.

community: The Raciborz Dolny dry polder was built on the land of two villages, Nieboczowy and Ligota Tworkowska. The completion report of 28 January 2021 says the process "included around 700 individuals belonging to about 250 households", and that "aside from the houses, church, and cemetery, all public facilities needed to be relocated". The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 10 June 2021 gives the same figures: "250 families were resettled, representing about 700 residents". A new village with all services was built for them near Syrynia, about 7 km from the old site. The appraisal document of 21 February 2007 records that the polder needed about 2,600 ha of land, that 20 businesses were in the polder area, most of which would be relocated or closed, and that 22 community assets would be closed or relocated, including a church, a chapel, seven crosses, five wayside shrines, a cemetery, two fire brigade buildings, a kindergarten, a school, a bread house, a recreation room and a sports club. Thirteen wayside shrines and conciliation crosses were moved to the new village. Most houses were bought by agreement over 2003 to 2012: the resettlement plan update of March 2015 counts about 68 buildings acquired by 2006, 1 in 2007, 14 in 2008, 11 in 2009, 8 in 2010, 16 in 2011 and 55 in 2012. In 2013, 30 houses were acquired under an administrative decision of the Silesian Voivodeship of 26 November 2012 rather than by agreement. Opposition was organised and long-running. A Committee for the Defence of Nieboczowy against Displacement was formally constituted in March 2002; the same plan update records 150 appeals against the location permit lodged with the Ministry of Infrastructure and 18 at the Administrative Court in Warsaw, with the Supreme Administrative Court rejecting the complaints on 27 April 2007. A 1998 survey of the two villages found that 91.9 per cent of those surveyed formally accepted displacement; the same plan update records that the survey met hostility and that ten households, 6 per cent, in Nieboczowy refused to answer it. A July 2002 survey of the same population, which followed a campaign by the defence committee urging residents not to co-operate, collected data from 70 per cent of households: 42.2 per cent gave express consent, 8.9 per cent had no opinion and 29.4 per cent refused outright. The same plan update records 74 property owners declaring a will to move in 2007 and 72 families willing to resettle as of April 2010. The completion report says there was "strong initial opposition, even leading to violent resistance", and that the project then built support through consultation; it says the resettled people "have indicated repeatedly that they are content with the new situation", and the Bank presents the resettlement as international best practice. RMF24 reported in April 2007 that about 200 residents were blocking the reservoir and would leave only if the whole village, including the church, was moved with them. The Catholic weekly Gosc Niedzielny reported on 30 June 2020, when the reservoir opened, that Nieboczowy's residents had jointly asked to be relocated and that the new village was built from scratch about 7 km away.
outcome: The polder was made operational in January 2020 and the reservoir was formally opened on 30 June 2020. The old village sites are inside the polder basin. The replacement village of Nieboczowy near Syrynia is built and occupied. Both the completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group rate the project's outcome Satisfactory.

title: Land taken from 38 people for four West Bank power substations, with compensation unfinished when the works began
place: Sarra village, Nablus Governorate, with almqeblih near Jenin, Beit Oula near Hebron and Qalandia near Ramallah, West Bank, Palestine

lenders.name: European Investment Bank
lenders.role: Financed the four 161/33/22 kV substations, which were Component 1 of the project the World Bank appraised and the component the land was taken for. The completion report lists Component 1 as "financed by EIB" and records an original EIB loan of EUR 45 million effective in 2005 that was originally to finance two of the four substations, EUR 10 million of meters and part of the new distribution system, and that EIB restructured during implementation; EIB then had to secure internal approval of a EUR 44.5 million single-source contract for the construction of the four substations by the Israel Electric Corporation, signed in February 2012. The component's actual cost is given as US$56.5 million, mostly EIB with Norwegian funding for some auxiliary equipment (completion report, paragraphs 13, 25 and 26, and the donor contributions table). The World Bank's own grants paid for other components: the central distribution system, distribution rehabilitation, capacity building, consultancies and the start-up costs of the new transmission company and regulator.

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Electric Utility Management Project, project number P084461, financed by two trust fund grants, TF-92336 and TF-94587. The original commitment was US$12.0 million and US$14.5 million was disbursed; the grant agreement for TF092336 is dated 30 June 2008 (Implementation Completion and Results Report, ICR00002455, 24 March 2017, data sheet and Annex 10). The Bank approved the project on 15 May 2008 and it closed on 30 September 2016, three years after the original closing date of 30 September 2013. The project was environmental Category B. The appraisal document's safeguard table marks two policies and only two: Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01) and Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12), with Natural Habitats, Pest Management, Physical Cultural Resources, Indigenous Peoples, Forests, Safety of Dams, Projects in Disputed Areas and Projects on International Waterways all marked no (Project Appraisal Document, report no. 43298-62, 22 April 2008, section III.F). The Bank appraised the four substations as Component 1 of the project, and the abbreviated resettlement action plans for each substation were prepared under the Resettlement Policy Framework that the Palestinian Energy Authority wrote in 2008 and under World Bank guidelines (completion report, paragraph 30). In September 2013 a Bank supervision mission found the Palestinian Energy and Natural Resources Authority non-compliant with Bank safeguard policies at three of the four substations, Jenin, Nablus and Hebron, because civil works had started before the Bank cleared and disclosed the environmental and resettlement instruments; the safeguards rating was upgraded to Moderately Satisfactory from Unsatisfactory in May 2014 and kept until closing (completion report, paragraph 30). In the same month a level-one restructuring adjusted the components, the objective and the indicators to the Bank-financed activities only. The Bank's Independent Evaluation Group records that the Bank "continued to monitor safeguard compliance related to the high-voltage substations even after restructuring when these activities no longer formed part of the project", and that Bank-managed financing accounted for less than 10 per cent of the cost of the original project (ICR Review, section 8b). The completion report rates the project's overall outcome Moderately Satisfactory. The Bank's Independent Evaluation Group rates the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory, on a split rating weighted by the 81 per cent of trust fund financing disbursed at restructuring, and rates risk to development outcome High (ICR Review, ICRR0020707, 2017, sections 6, 7 and 11a).

companies.name: Palestinian Energy and Natural Resources Authority
companies.role: Implementing agency, the Palestinian Authority body responsible for the energy sector; its Project Management Unit ran the project. Its Land Acquisition Committee assessed the price of each parcel and a Land Evaluation Committee valued the land against neighbouring parcel prices; the expropriation decrees required cabinet approval and confirmation by the office of the president. This is the body the Bank's September 2013 mission found non-compliant with its safeguard policies at three of the four substations (completion report, paragraph 30; Resettlement Action Plan, March 2011, sections 2.2 and 2.3).

companies.name: Israel Electric Corporation
companies.role: Built the four substations under a single-source contract approved by the European Investment Bank. The completion report says the Palestinian Authority and EIB concluded that only this company could effectively build the substations in the West Bank, because of the complexity of the approval processes from the Israeli authorities and the need to deal with them, and that it took from May 2008 to October 2010 to agree contract terms, partly because the company had no obvious interest in speeding up construction, which would cut its short-term electricity sales to the West Bank (completion report, paragraph 25).

community: Four high-voltage substations needed land at four sites. The project's Resettlement Action Plan of March 2011 names them and counts the people whose land was taken. At Jenin, 15,028 square metres were taken from 23 owners, including, in the plan's spelling, owners of almqeblih village; the plan says that process 'has already been conducted by Palestinian industrial Zone', that the ownership of the 15,028 square metres 'is transferred to PEA', and that JD 66,315.20, assessed at JD 4.41 per square metre, 'has to be paid for the 23 owner'. So the Jenin land was taken through the industrial zone and transferred on, not acquired by the energy authority itself. At Sarra village in Nablus Governorate, 15,174 square metres belonging to 10 owners, with JD 349,000 assessed at JD 23 per square metre to be paid. At Beit Oula village near Hebron, about 17,524 square metres from 4 owners, with JD 89,898 assessed at JD 5.13 per square metre to be paid. At Qalandia, 11,000 square metres bought directly, with one person listed as affected and no price yet set. The plan's summary table lists the four sites with 23, 10, 4 and 1 persons affected. It records the status of each: the Jenin process 'finish', Sarra and Beit Oula awaiting cabinet approval, Qalandia still at the estimation stage. The plan's two accounts of the Jenin site do not agree. Its summary table marks the Jenin status 'Resettlement process finish', while its annexed compensation table for the same three parcels enters 23 owners and JD 66,315.2 in the column for the amount awarded to owners, leaves the expropriation decree number and the expropriation date blank, and reads in the comments column: 'Assessed amount not yet awarded'. That annex also names each owner, with the parcel, the land title number, the area in dunams and a column for the owner's national identity card number: 23 people at Jenin across parcels 8/1, 10/1 and 11/1, in Almqebleh title 20010 and Berqin title 2, plus a 0.468-dunam road strip. The plan also lists tentative dates for Citizen Consultancy Meetings, Qalandia in September 2011 and Jenin, Nablus and Hebron in June 2012, after the assessments had been made; it describes those meetings as gathering community feedback on the configuration of the distribution system rather than on the land acquisition. For Sarra and Beit Oula the plan says notices with the owners' names and land titles were published twice in local newspapers and that no owner objected. The plan says the land was taken by expropriation under the 1953 Land Acquisition Law, applied in the West Bank from Jordanian legislation, and that it remains hard to seek remedies in the Palestinian court system because of uncertainty over enforcement and the limits of a court system operating under occupation. The project's completion report of 24 March 2017 records what happened next: at Jenin, Nablus and Hebron, civil works began before the Bank had cleared and disclosed the resettlement and environmental instruments, and 'project affected people were identified prior to construction and the compensation process had started but it had not yet been completed'. The same paragraph says the issue was solved thanks to the proactivity of the Bank team and for the benefit of EIB, and that the safeguards rating was upgraded in May 2014. A footnote to that paragraph records that the Bank's Jerusalem office received a complaint by email from the closest neighbour to the Nablus substation; the task team met the complainant, four other neighbours and the mayor, raised their concerns with the Palestinian authority and EIB, and sent the complainant a written response. The footnote does not say what the complaint was about. The areas, the owner counts and the assessed sums appear in that plan and in no outcome document. outcome: The project closed on 30 September 2016. Three of the four substations were complete at closing; the fourth, at Ramallah, was 15 per cent complete, held up by permits from the Israeli authorities for works in Area C, and was planned for commissioning in July 2018. The two reports do not agree on where the compensation ended up. The completion report says the compensation process had started but had not yet been completed when the works began, and that the issue was solved. The Independent Evaluation Group's review says the completion report reports that the non-compliance issues "had been rectified by closure", while adding that it does not state whether there was compliance with OP 4.01, and reads the same page as meaning that 'although project affected people were identified prior to the commencement of construction activities, the compensation process had not been completed by project closure', adds that the task team leader subsequently informed the Group that the process was later completed, and says the completion report does not state whether the compensation and resettlement processes conformed to the requirements of OP 4.12. companies.role: Ran the project through a Single Project Implementation Unit shared with the Rural Sector Support Project, which prepared the resettlement plans, paid compensation and set up 15 grievance committees. The ministry paid the burial costs for one of the two people who died.

title: Deaths and Unapproved Displacement on the Mafinga-Igawa Road
place: Mafinga-Igawa road, Iringa and Mbeya regions, Tanzania

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Southern Africa Trade and Transport Facilitation Project, first phase (P120370), Credit IDA-52480 of SDR 138.7 million (US$210 million equivalent) to Tanzania and Grant IDA-H8440 of SDR 2.0 million (US$3 million) to the Dar es Salaam Corridor Committee, approved 21 May 2013, effective 26 November 2013, closed 31 December 2020 after two extensions; US$175.4 million disbursed. The rehabilitation of the 137.9 km Mafinga-Igawa section of the Dar es Salaam corridor took 78 per cent of the project's money; for the remaining stretch to the Zambian border at Tunduma the project paid only for feasibility studies, detailed designs and safeguard instruments. The project also financed a one-stop border post at Songwe/Kasumulu on the Malawi border, an inspection station at Vigwaza and works at eight accident black spots. The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory and Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory (28 January 2022); the Evaluation Group rates Bank performance and the quality of supervision Moderately Unsatisfactory, records that the project closed with a moderately unsatisfactory rating for safeguards, and says it is not clear how the Bank "addressed the issue of fatalities related to contractors and ensured that such accidents did not repeat".

companies.name: Tanzania National Roads Agency (TANROADS)
companies.role: Implementing agency for the road works, the border post and the black spot works; began work at one black spot, including displacing people, without preparing the safeguard documents

community: Twenty-four people died along the Mafinga-Igawa road while it was being rehabilitated. The completion report counts 104 accidents on the project road during construction, 13 of them fatal, and says that of the 24 deaths "two were attributed to the contractors' employees or involved contractors' employees and/or equipment, with the rest due to road crashes". The report puts the rate at 0.06 deaths per kilometre per year, half the Tanzanian average of 0.11 for trunk roads at the time, which it links to the slower speeds through the works, and then calls that rate "undoubtedly shocking". A road safety audit was carried out and its findings went into the road design. The borrower's comments, printed in the same report, dispute the Bank's account: they give the number as 23, say that calling it a large number "is not evidenced", point out that the report itself records the rate as below the national average, and say there is no evidence for the implied conclusion that the contractors' handling of traffic was insufficient for the traffic on the corridor. On land, the report says resettlement plans were prepared and carried out satisfactorily for most of the works, but that problems remained at closing in two places. At the one-stop border post, "compensation and demolition of property required by the implementation occurred prior to clearance of the RAP". At one of the black spot sites, "works began, including displacement without preparation of safeguards instruments by TANROADS and approval by the WB". The Bank says it kept monitoring after the project closed to ensure its resettlement policy was met and the affected people properly compensated, and that it will do so until all the resettlement issues are addressed. Other safeguard failures the report and the review record are a contractor dumping debris in wetlands and blocking water flow, and diversion roads built for the works left unattended, with erosion then affecting more than 20 km along the corridor.

The time for trucks to cross from Songwe into Malawi rose from 24 hours at appraisal to 72 hours at closing, which the report puts down to the construction still under way and to Covid-19 controls. The resettlement and compensation problems at the border post and at the black spot were unresolved when the project closed, and the project's safeguards rating at closing was Moderately Unsatisfactory.

lenders.role: Zanzibar Urban Services Project (P111155), Credit IDA-48610 of US$38 million approved 24 February 2011 and Credit IDA-58430 of US$55 million as additional financing in June 2016, SDR 63.9 million in all; US$87.57 million disbursed; closed 31 May 2021, five years after its first closing date. community: Five people died in three accidents on the drainage works between 2015 and 2020. The completion report says the project "encountered weaknesses on the implementation of health and safety issues which led to three severe accidents and five fatalities". A trespasser who broke into a drainage work site through a gap in the fence fell and drowned on 3 April 2016. Two workers died when the soil collapsed at a deep cut on 8 November 2019. Two passengers on a motorcycle died when it crashed into a dump truck working near the Mwanakwerekwe pond on 22 March 2020. After each accident the project team took statements from contractors, workers, consultants and other witnesses, reported to the lender, and agreed corrective measures; the report says site safety and health management improved after those measures. On land and money, the drainage designs were revised during the project and the number of people affected and the cost came out far above the plan; the government could not pay and no land was available for land-for-land swaps, so the credit paid instead. The report says 605 people were compensated for the drainage and solid waste works, "albeit with some delays". A further 167 people in the buffer zone of the Kibele landfill faced delays and incomplete payment because the government budget ran short; after the lender released another US$550,000, all but three had been paid by 1 April 2021. A footnote records that those three could not be reached through radio, newspapers, village leaders "and so on", and that after the loan account closed at the end of September 2021 the government is obliged to pay them if they come forward to claim. The resettlement plan of December 2018 for drainage system C counted 194 affected households and 162 structures, 30 of them to be taken completely: 141 residential structures, of which 30 would be taken entirely and 111 would lose a wall, a verandah, a foundation, a room, a toilet, an outside kitchen or a septic tank; 12 businesses to be closed and moved, among them six at Sogea and shops at Shaurimoyo, Jitimai and Magogoni; and shelters used by widows, disabled people and people with long illnesses who the plan says would need help to move. The November 2017 plan for the Kibele landfill counted 60 individual landholders, of whom 13 living in occupied dwellings, with 57 household members, were to be moved out of the project area. The municipal council demolished one house, with compensation, to open a route for collection vehicles into a dense settlement where people had been throwing their rubbish into the drain. The Evaluation Group also records that the existing dump site, which the project had assumed would last five years, was closed during the project by community opposition unconnected to the project, after which the council "began open dumping of waste in Ng'ambo settlements causing an environmental and public health crisis".
outcome: The project closed on 31 May 2021 with an outcome rating of Satisfactory. Three people in the Kibele landfill buffer zone had still not been paid when the loan account closed at the end of September 2021, and the government was notified of its obligation to pay them in future. The completion report says overall safeguards management, occupational health and site safety improved after the accidents.

community: The project rebuilt part of the M-03 Kyiv-Kharkiv-Dovzhanskyi road and built three bypasses in Poltava oblast: Pokrovska Bahachka, Krasnohorivka and the first stage of the Poltava bypass. The addendum of 9 December 2017 records a house damaged by the works. It says: "No physical resettlement was induced at any stage of the acquisition. However, one PAP in Krasnogorivka bypass has now approached the local administration for resettlement through replacement of house in the same village (Bilotserkivka) as the walls of the house developed cracks due to ongoing road construction works in the RoW about 10 meters away from the house." The same paragraph says the case "was reviewed, found deserving, and is being considered eligible for relocation and resettlement assistance" under the original plan's entitlement matrix, and that the person was added to the list of affected people because the approved plan had not identified them. Addendum No.2, dated December 2018 on its cover, records an acquisition at the same village for a different reason. It says a design change made after residents and local authorities asked for two cattle passes and local roads so people could move around the village without using the main road "resulted in need for additional acquisition of 3 land plots, 1 house and involuntary resettlement of 1 person in the Bilotserkivka village". It does not mention the cracked walls, and no document says the house acquired is the house that cracked. Its table of the three plots names the owners: two plots registered to Nechay O., one for individual housing, a garage and dacha construction and one for personal farming, and one to the company LLC Lubny ShBU No.9. It then sets out the case in detail. Oleksiy Nechay, born 1940, retired and living on a pension, owns the plot with the house on it; the house is 60 square metres, built in the 1960s, with a summer kitchen beside it. He gave his grandson Sharay Artem power of attorney on 30 August 2018 to negotiate the price and sale, and the grandson was to buy him accommodation in Poltava and move him there himself, so the addendum records that no further relocation help from the road service was needed. The addendum also says that as of 2 October 2018 the contractor had the owners' written consent "to carry out civil works on their land plots before the payment of compensation", and that no works were being done on the plot holding the house. The counts of affected people do not agree between the two addenda. Addendum No.1 gives 106 in the original 2012 plan rising to 124 as of 30 November 2017, covering 113.8947 hectares and an estimated 70,245,919 hryvnia of compensation. Addendum No.2 gives 121 as of the same date, and 122 as of 31 October 2018, reached by adding two affected people on the Bilotserkivka lot and subtracting one on the Poltava bypass, where a plot found to have three heirs was counted as one after they were paid in equal shares. Neither document explains the difference between 124 and 121. The 2017 addendum also records that the grievance system agreed in the loan agreement was not working: "Establishment of GRM procedures for the project as agreed in the Loan agreement and approved RAP was not fully executed due to various constraints including jurisdictional authority to enforce the same." It says awareness of the mechanism among people in the project area "is very low", that dissemination by the local administration "has been very limited", and that this "has led to an increase in the number of grievances submitted when road construction works commenced". Some people went to the administration or the courts instead. The completion report says the resettlement policy was triggered because the works "required land acquisition causing both physical and economic displacement", that the involuntary resettlement rating was downgraded for periods "due to lack of attentiveness and initiatives on the part of the agencies involved in land acquisition to resolve issues", and that it was later upgraded. The same paragraph says social safeguard compliance "was mainly rated as satisfactory and social impact and risk related to land acquisition and resettlement was assessed as moderate".
outcome: The road and the bypasses were built and the project closed on 30 June 2021. The completion report says the land acquisition problem that mattered most was the delay in government reimbursement, which was resolved when the Bank agreed to finance the acquisitions from the loan. It records no outcome for the damaged house.

title: Pump station built on a Bukhara household's plot before any plan existed

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Project P112719, Bukhara and Samarkand Sewerage Project. IDA credit 4633-UZ (US$55 million, financing and project agreements conformed 26 November 2009) and additional financing credits 5698-UZ and 5699-UZ (agreements 13 May 2016). Approved 4 August 2009, effective 1 April 2010, closed 30 November 2021 against an original closing date of 31 December 2015; US$132.85 million disbursed of a US$136.82 million project. The completion report of 31 May 2022 rates the overall outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the environmental and social safeguards performance at closing Moderately Satisfactory.

companies.name: Bukhara Regional Production State Enterprise Suvokova
companies.role: The regional state water and sewerage utility for Bukhara, the employer for the Bukhara works and a party to the project agreement with the Bank. The plan calls it the Employer for the contract to rehabilitate the existing sewers in Bukhara city.

community: The resettlement action plan of 18 May 2012, for the contract to rehabilitate existing sewers in Bukhara city, covers a wastewater pumping station of 12 metres by 12 metres, 144 square metres, and the sewer lines running to it. The land it was built on was being used by a householder the plan names as Toychiev Nurjon, of Sitora street number 50, who had no authorised document for it. The plan says the use of the site was granted to the utility by decision number 1067 of 24 August 2010 of the Khokim of Bukhara city, "but unfortunately the nearby householder was informed only verbally about the project". By the time the plan was written the clearing had already happened. It says about 30 metres of the existing fence and the steel entrance gate "have already been dismantled by the contractor with the assistance of the householder worker and stored in the householder stores", and that the brick storage house "was demolished" and its roof, doors and windows and the chicken shelter dismantled and stored the same way. The plot held an old chain-link fence enclosing 1,200 square metres with a steel gate, the fence 88 metres long and 2.5 metres high; a brick store 3.8 by 3.8 by 2.4 metres with a corrugated asbestos roof; a closed steel chicken house; and shrubs, vegetation and trees, for which the plan says there is no accurate count. Because no survey of the planting was done before the works, the compensation was worked backwards from an assumed maximum. The plan says the Bukhara City Beautification Department, as a third party, set the maximum at 21 young plants, and the calculation uses cherry, "the most valuable from the list of fruit trees submitted by the owner": 5 kilograms a year over six years, times 21 trees, times the three years taken for trees to grow back, 1,890 kilograms at 1,200 soums a kilogram, 2,268,000 soums, plus 315,000 soums of labour and gardening costs, 2,583,000 soums for the planting, and a disturbance and inconvenience allowance of 10 per cent on top, 258,300 soums, for a total compensation to the household of 2,841,300 soums. The plan says the store, chicken shelter, fence and gate were to be rebuilt by the utility to a layout agreed with the household, that the contractor was to restore the land, that the household would then be able to cultivate the land around the pumping station, and that the household said no temporary shelter or store was needed while the work went on. An annex to the plan is the household's signed receipt for the cash part of the compensation. The project's resettlement policy framework states that "all compensation and other entitlements will need to be paid prior to proceeding with the civil works", which at this site did not happen. It also says the location of the station was adjusted in consultation with the household to reduce the loss of planting. The completion report of 31 May 2022 says the project had no large-scale resettlement and that most of the works were inside existing facilities or along roads, that four resettlement action plans were prepared and carried out "with adequate compensation paid to project-affected parties by project closing", and then: "However, during implementation, inconsistencies in social safeguard policies were a challenge. For example, there were instances of project-affected persons not being compensated for project impacts on time due to lack of capacity to prepare and implement the Resettlement Action Plans."
outcome: The project closed on 30 November 2021 after two extensions. The completion report says the four resettlement plans were carried out and compensation paid by closing, with no pending actions, and rates safeguards Moderately Satisfactory. It does not say which affected people were paid late, or how late.

title: Farm land taken for drainage works before the resettlement plan covered it
place: Bagdad, Rishtan and Altiaryk districts, Fergana region, Uzbekistan

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Ferghana Valley Water Resources Management Project Phase I, P110538, credit IDA-46480. Approved 24 September 2009, closed 31 December 2016. XDR 33.76 million disbursed. The safeguards compliance rating was downgraded during implementation over the land acquisition and later upgraded. The completion report of 16 May 2017 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, as does the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 16 October 2017.

companies.name: Projects Implementation Unit for Water Infrastructure, Ministry of Agriculture and Water Resources of Uzbekistan
companies.role: The unit inside the national water ministry that ran the project, prepared the resettlement plans and the land acquisition reports, and operated the grievance mechanism. Compensation amounts were set by decisions of the Fergana regional governor (khakim) and the district governors.

community: Rehabilitating drainage and irrigation canals took farm land, permanently and temporarily, and removed trees along roads, canals and drains. The resettlement plan prepared before appraisal and updated in 2011 covered 37 farmers. The completion report of 16 May 2017 says that "between 2012 and 2014, 338 farmers were affected by the project activities, and land acquisition took place without the RAP being updated, which constituted a noncompliance with the World Bank OP 4.12", because local authorities would not approve updates until the list of farmers was final. The report also says that "compensation payments were done with delay after land acquisition and/or civil works started", blaming invalid bank details and suspended bank accounts, and that "in most cases, the PAPs did not receive any cash as compensation was used to settle outstanding tax arrears". It adds that some farmers who were paid turned out not to be affected at all, and that there was no mechanism to recover those payments. The borrower's own report on land acquisition in 2012 to 2014, dated November 2015, puts figures to it and explains most of the gaps. Four decisions of the Fergana regional governor between October 2011 and April 2014 covered 513 farm enterprises in all. Under the first, of 10 October 2011, all 37 enterprises listed were paid in full. Under the decision of 13 December 2013, damage to 189 enterprises was assessed at UZS 611,791,000 and UZS 512,663,126 was paid to 155 of them; of the 34 unpaid, 10 had suffered no damage because part of the collector works was dropped at detailed design, and the money for the remaining 24 came back because their bank details were wrong. Under the decision of 15 February 2014, the report's text says damage to 62 enterprises was assessed at UZS 127,215,230 and UZS 126,246,030 was paid to 60 of them, the other two held up by incorrect bank accounts, while the report's own summary table lists 128 enterprises under the same decision with 60 paid; both readings are in the one document. Under the decision of 15 April 2014, the text says UZS 235,988,691 was paid to 121 land users and that of the remaining 38, 28 had suffered no damage during construction and 10 had money returned over bank details, while the summary table gives 123 paid. The table's total is 373 paid of 513, and the report accounts for the 140 difference as 36 farmers awaiting correct banking details and 104 farmers who were not harmed because the work was done before planting and after harvest; the table's own rows sum to 375 rather than 373. A further decision of 25 December 2014 assessed damage of UZS 494,989,548 and the report says no payment had been made under it because funds had to be reallocated. The report puts total damage under the project at UZS 1,918 million, of which UZS 937,803,509 was paid in 2011 to 2014 and UZS 980,473,630 was still to be paid by the end of 2015, a balance that includes the UZS 436.35 million it estimates for 2015 and not only arrears to the farmers already assessed. Land taken ran 515.25 ha in 2012 and 197.49 ha in 2015; for 2013 the report's text gives 358 ha while its table for the same year totals 334.51 ha, and for 2014 it gives 334.52 ha under one contract and a further 226.57 ha under another. The completion report says all outstanding payments were made before the project closed, and that the use of compensation against tax arrears "did not seem to cause any unhappiness in the farmers' community".
outcome: The drainage works were built and the project closed in December 2016 with the outstanding compensation paid, according to the completion report. The Independent Evaluation Group's field-based Project Performance Assessment Report of 29 March 2019 records both sides of the compliance question: its safeguards section says "overall, the project complied with the implementation of safeguards" and that "previous reviews of the safeguards confirmed full compliance", while its assessment of the implementing agency says the project unit was understaffed for environmental and social safeguards, which "partly led to noncompliance with both", and that issues over approval of the resettlement action plan and delays in compensation payments to project-affected people "persisted for some time, causing the downgrade in safeguards performance ratings".

title: Land and Crops Taken for a Road Realignment Before the Resettlement Policy Applied
place: The Hopewell to Teviot road, between Hopewell and Richland Park, Mesopotamia valley, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-48520 (4852-VC) for the Hurricane Tomas Emergency Recovery Project (P124939), SDR 3.30 million, US$5 million equivalent, of which SDR 3.11 million was disbursed. Borrower the Government of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines; implementing agency the Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning. Lending instrument an emergency recovery loan, environmental category B. Approved 13 January 2011, effective 4 May 2011, mid-term review 22 January 2013, closed 31 December 2013. The project was restructured on 26 August 2013 to trigger Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12), which had not been triggered at appraisal, after works had already taken land. The completion report ICR00003178, dated 30 June 2014 on its cover and 25 June 2014 in its data sheet, rated outcome Satisfactory, risk to development outcome Moderate, Bank performance Satisfactory and borrower performance Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR14666, posted 21 November 2014, agreed on outcome and on Bank performance but rated the risk to development outcome Significant rather than Moderate, because budgets for maintenance are generally inadequate and the line ministries' financial and capacity constraints are likely to hamper long-term maintenance.

companies.name: Ministry of Transport, Works, Urban Development and Local Government
companies.role: The ministry whose works took the land. The remedial plan records that it asked two landowners' permission to "cut Land" to realign a section of Hopewell Road, and that it and the contractors proceeded under national procedures that did not require them to inform the Central Planning Division, because the Bank's resettlement policy had not been triggered. Its Chief Engineer was the ministry's representative on the project, responsible for minor civil works and supervision and for defining the project area (Remedial Abbreviated Resettlement Action Plan, 14 March 2013; Resettlement Policy Framework, May 2013).

companies.name: Central Planning Division, Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning
companies.role: The unit inside the finance ministry that manages the project and its safeguards, and that notified the Bank of the land acquisition on 30 November 2012 once it had established the extent of the impacts. Under the policy framework it is responsible for procurement, financial management, monitoring and evaluation and payment of compensation (Remedial Abbreviated Resettlement Action Plan, 14 March 2013; Resettlement Policy Framework, May 2013).

community:
The project front-loaded repairs to infrastructure damaged by Hurricane Tomas, which struck in October 2010. The works picked for it were already known to the government and the Bank and were not expected to need any land acquisition, so the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy was not triggered and no resettlement framework or action plan existed.

During work on the Hopewell Road, soil erosion from heavy rainfall in October 2012 forced a change of engineering design, and the new design took land. A survey by the Lands and Surveys Department in September 2012 found encroachment on two properties, one on either side of the road: 3,064 square feet, which the plan puts at 40 per cent of that owner's assets, and 297 square feet, 1 per cent of the other's. Four people, in two families of two, were recorded as directly affected. The Central Planning Division told the Bank on 30 November 2012.

A Bank mission on 5 to 7 December 2012 visited the site, confirmed the encroachment and set out the steps for consulting and compensating the two owners. The same mission found the revised retaining-wall design inadequate, and on 22 December 2012 the Bank told the Director of Planning that the sub-project should be suspended until an acceptable design was produced. The Bank then began a restructuring to trigger the resettlement policy and asked the government to prepare a remedial abbreviated resettlement action plan and a resettlement policy framework.

The remedial plan, dated 14 March 2013, records what was agreed. Both owners chose cash. Compensation for crops was recorded as finalised on 5 March 2013, with values set from Ministry of Agriculture rates; payment for the temporary loss of use of agricultural land and of its productivity had been effected. The two payments for the land itself are recorded as "Awaiting payment", with June 2013 as the expected completion date. The plan's per-person table leaves each land valuation as "value tbd", while its budget table estimates the cost of compensation at XCD 15,570.00 for the 3,361 square feet of land and XCD 5,812.58 for the crops, both to be met by the government out of the Consolidated Fund. The plan notes that there is no provision for land-for-land compensation in the law of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, though it happens in practice case by case. The second owner's private pathway was used as a public right of way while the road was closed; no money was asked for, and instead five street lights were installed along 200 feet of road, officers were assigned from the Mesopotamia Police Station, and the public was urged to respect the property. In consultation the affected people "indicated the need for full and fair compensation of property and crops in a timely manner", and welcomed the gabion baskets supporting their land and crops and the benefit of a stabilised road.

The completion report puts the encroachment at 3,361 square feet in total and says it "did not have a substantial impact on the two affected land owners, nor on the community", and that the Bank, within two weeks of being told, sent a team that helped the government address the consultation and compensation and "effectively address[ed] the problem on the ground". At a second site, the Rillan Hill Community Centre, nearby residents had planted crops before works began; it was decided that no compensation was needed because the crops were harvested first.
outcome: The credit closed on 31 December 2013 with SDR 3.11 million of SDR 3.30 million disbursed. No document found records the two payments for the land being made; the only figure for them is the plan's budget estimate of XCD 15,570.00. The completion report, six months after the plan's own June 2013 deadline, says the Bank assisted the government in addressing the compensation and that the problem was effectively addressed, but gives no amounts and no date of payment. The remedial plan was disclosed in the country on 12 July 2013 and sent for public disclosure on 16 July 2013, and the project was restructured on 26 August 2013 to trigger the resettlement policy. The mid-term review recommended that the implementation unit's fiduciary and safeguard compliance be strengthened.

title: Shala neighbourhood cleared for lignite mining, and years in temporary housing
place: Shala neighbourhood of Hade village, Obiliq municipality, Kosovo

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Energy Sector Clean-up and Land Reclamation Project, P096181, grants IDA-H2340 and IDA-H3190 and credit IDA-52400, with trust funds TF-13509 and TF-90160. Approved 13 June 2006, closed 31 August 2016. The second additional financing, approved 10 May 2013 and filed separately as P131539, added US$4.2 million and created Component F, which paid for monitoring of the Resettlement Action Plan for the Shala neighbourhood. The completion report of 28 February 2017 rates the outcome Satisfactory, as does the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 29 June 2017. The completion report states that the project "did not cause nor finance the resettlement; it only supervised MESP's responsibility to implement the RAP". The Resettlement Action Plan itself was a technical assistance output of another Bank-financed project, the Lignite Power Technical Assistance Project, in 2011.

lenders.name: Netherlands Ministry for Development Cooperation
lenders.role: Co-financier. A grant of US$4.33 million agreed in December 2006 covered the original project's financing gap, and a second grant of US$1.2 million came with the second additional financing (completion report, 28 February 2017).

companies.name: Korporata Energjetike e Kosoves (KEK)
companies.role: Kosovo's energy corporation, which the completion report's abbreviation list writes as "Kosovo Energy Cooperation". It operates the Kosovo A and Kosovo B lignite power plants and the mines that supply them; the project was designed in part to build capacity inside it for clean-up and mining operations. Its mine expansion took the land of the Shala neighbourhood, and it paid the compensation and the temporary rent allowances.

companies.name: Ministry of Environment and Spatial Planning of Kosovo (MESP)
companies.role: The ministry responsible for implementing the Shala Resettlement Action Plan, including building the water, sewage and electricity infrastructure at the resettlement site. It ran the grievance commission, which the resettlement completion report says stopped working.

companies.name: rePlan Inc.
companies.role: The international resettlement consultancy commissioned to prepare the Shala Resettlement Action Plan and then, under the Bank-financed Component F, to monitor and report on its implementation.

community: KEK's lignite mine expansion took the Shala neighbourhood of Hade village. The resettlement completion report of July 2016 counts 93 affected households: 63 of them, with 320 full-time residents, were resident households that "needed to be physically displaced", and the other 30 lost land only. By June 2015 the report records 0 of the 63 households still living in Shala. In January 2012, 21 of the 93 households were found to be in a risk zone, were required to leave at once, and were given a monthly rent and living allowance. The Inspection Panel visited the site in 2015 and its Report and Recommendation of 2 September 2015 records residents saying they had been living in temporary housing since 2011 or 2012 because the resettlement site was not ready, and that only in late 2014 did they receive their plots. The same residents told the Panel that the food allowance and emergency rent assistance they had been given during the temporary relocation was discontinued in April 2014 even though the site was not yet ready and many households were still in rented housing. The Panel team recorded its own observations of the incomplete sewerage and the poor condition of the secondary roads at the site. The Bank's completion report says the resettlement was in breach of the Resettlement Action Plan and of the project's legal covenants by December 2013, and that the Bank threatened to suspend disbursements; the breach was resolved when KEK approved more rent payments for the 21 families. The report also records untimely payment of the temporary rent allowances as putting the project in bad standing with its legal covenants. Rebuilding was slow. The resettlement completion report counts 52 of 52 plots allocated with title deeds issued by June 2015, 48 of 52 construction permits issued, 22 plots with construction started or finished, 15 of those 22 houses ready to live in and 12 occupied, with 53 people living at the new site. The same report gives its own explanation for the 30 allocated plots not built on: informal engagements with households revealed that many had opted to stay in the temporary accommodation they had taken in Pristina, while others chose to buy or build elsewhere, and some judged the resettlement site incomplete. Three houses that were ready stood empty in February 2016 because the sewage collecting pipe was blocked. Residents reported 50 metres of blocked sewage pipe in October 2015 and the ministry estimated that about 200 metres needed replacing. Three of the 30 households that lost land only had still not claimed their compensation in February 2016. The 2015 survey ran 32 interviews covering 38 of the 93 affected households, a sample the report puts at 40.8 per cent with a margin of error of 10 points. In it, 43.8 per cent said their economic situation was worse than a year before, against 23.1 per cent in 2011; in the same table the share saying it was better rose from 7.7 per cent to 25 per cent and the share saying it was the same fell from 67.3 to 31.2 per cent. Among the households that lost land without moving, 62.5 per cent said they were worse off, against 37.5 per cent of those physically displaced. The same report concludes that "livelihoods and living conditions have been at least restored and in some instances improved", and that compensation complied with the Bank's resettlement policy. Residents told the Inspection Panel a different story: that compensation was set on a 2004 valuation, that they had to pay the difference between the value of their old plots and the new ones, which they put at about 12,500 euros, that their new plots were smaller, that 20 jobs KEK was to provide under a 2011 agreement had not all materialised, that there was no school or clinic near the site, and that they had never been told of any grievance mechanism.
outcome: The Shala neighbourhood is gone and the mine has expanded over it. The Inspection Panel investigated and its report went to the Bank's board in 2016. The Bank's management agreed to three follow-up actions: repairing a 200-metre section of clogged sewage, technical assistance to revise the resettlement policy framework, and a workshop with the government and KEK. The completion report says the sewage was repaired by December 2016 and the workshop was held on 14 February 2017, and notes that only the sewage repair is directly linked to the project. At the project's closing in August 2016, 12 of the 52 households that chose a plot at the new site were living there. In September 2016 KEK opened negotiations with several hundred more residents who are to be moved for new excavations.

title: Market Traders Moved at Kasumbalesa Border Post
place: Kasumbalesa border post, Chililabombwe District, Copperbelt Province, Zambia

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Road Rehabilitation and Maintenance Project (P071985), SDR 33.5 million (US$50 million equivalent) approved 9 March 2004, with a first additional financing of SDR 16.8 million (US$25 million) and a second of SDR 9.9 million (US$15 million); the completion report's cover gives the credit numbers as IDA-38660, IDA-38661 and IDPA-48210. SDR 59.98 million was disbursed. The project closed on 30 June 2014, seven years after its first closing date. The credit paid for the rehabilitation of the Chingola-Kasumbalesa road and for its engineering supervision; the completion report gives the length rehabilitated as 39 km in its results annex and as 40.5 km in its outputs annex, and the Evaluation Group's review gives the road as 40 km. The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the implementing agencies' performance Moderately Unsatisfactory (27 April 2015); the Independent Evaluation Group rates the outcome, Bank performance and borrower performance all Moderately Unsatisfactory.

companies.name: Chililabombwe Municipal Council
companies.role: Its Engineering Section moved the traders, found the new sites and valued what they lost

companies.name: Road Development Agency
companies.role: Implementing agency for the road works and the channel through which the compensation receipts were to be passed to the lender

community: In December 2005 traders were moved from the north-eastern side of the Chingola-Kasumbalesa road to the western side, to clear space for trucks waiting to be cleared by immigration at the border. The Environmental Management Unit of the Roads Department, which was responsible for applying the lender's resettlement rules, was told only after the move had happened. The abbreviated resettlement plan written afterwards, in May 2006, states that "because of lack of information and sensitization, the provisions outlined in the Resettlement Policy Framework completed during project preparation have not been followed", and that the plan was written to correct that. The plan lists 67 numbered traders by name and national registration number, some names appearing more than once, and puts the number of people at roughly 65: 23 restaurants, 20 grocery stalls, 21 sellers of vegetables, fruit and other goods, one carpentry business and two pay phones. The sums set were 2,590,000 kwacha for each restaurant, 1,390,000 for each grocery, 400,000 for each market seller, 250,000 for the carpentry and 8,000,000 for each pay phone, 113,410,000 kwacha in all. The costs counted were taking down and rebuilding structures, buying materials, business lost during the move, and transport of materials from Chililabombwe 20 km away. The plan says the host community was the same community, because the move was within the same area, and that the facilities used before the move still served the people who were resettled. The Evaluation Group's review of the completion report says the government's counterpart funding "was not paid on schedule, only six percent of the required commitments per year, causing delays in implementing the Resettlement Action Plan (RAP), and thus negatively impacting the overall project implementation timetable and costs". The same passage adds that the counterpart funding "was fully realized (US$64.3 million) at project closure as per commitment", and the review rates government performance Moderately Satisfactory.
outcome: The plan set out that the contractor would pay each trader in front of a council officer and an officer of the Environmental Management Unit, that each would sign a receipt, and that the signed receipts would go to the Resident Engineer as part of the contractor's monthly claim and on to the Road Development Agency, the National Road Fund Agency and the World Bank. Neither the completion report nor the Evaluation Group's review of it says whether the money was paid. The completion report's table of safeguard documents records the abbreviated plan as disclosed in July 2006. The road was rehabilitated; the Evaluation Group's review says that at closing several sections, among them Chingola-Kasumbalesa, were in poor condition and in further need of repair.

title: Fifty-seven households moved for the Mufuchani bridge at Kitwe

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Second Phase of the Road Rehabilitation and Maintenance Project (P106596), Credit IDA-46540, Credit Number 4654-ZA, approved 16 October 2009, agreement dated 25 November 2009. The completion report of 26 October 2016 rates safeguards compliance Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 1 May 2017 repeats the completion report's account of the resettlement.

companies.name: Road Development Agency, Zambia
companies.role: The roads agency under the Ministry of Works and Supply that commissioned the bridge and prepared the Mufuchani Resettlement Action Plan of February 2009. Its Environmental and Social Management Unit, set up under the national road programme ROADSIP, monitored the works.

community: The credit paid for a new bridge over the Kafue River at Mufuchani, to link the Mufuchani farming area to Kitwe. Before the bridge there was no motorised crossing; the nearest route was about 10 km away. The resettlement plan of February 2009 records 57 households whose homes stood fully in the way, 55 of them in the Ipusukilo Stage III settlement and 2 on the Mufuchani farming block, and three more properties partly affected, being two churches and one house. It counts 333 affected people, 27 landlords, 21 food stalls to be helped to move, 370 fruit trees, one farm plot of 248 square metres and two crop plots totalling 64 square metres. The completion report records what was built: "57 new houses, two churches, and a 1.5 km access road were constructed in Kitwe in the Copperbelt Province", with water, sewerage and electricity connected "to ensure smooth relocation of project affected people". The Times of Zambia, in a report published on 18 January 2014, described the handover the day before of 57 houses and two churches in the Kawama and Ipusukilo townships of Kitwe, at a cost of K17 million, built under the Mufuchani Resettlement Action Programme with World Bank funding, and quoted the works minister saying the government wanted to provide decent housing for the affected families. The completion report says the project complied with all safeguard policies and that no major environmental or social safeguards issue arose during it.
outcome: The bridge was finished on 31 January 2016 and 371,570 vehicles a year crossed it, against a target of 60,000. The documents record no complaint from the households moved, and no later figure for what they lost. In January 2016 the Times of Zambia reported that Kitwe City Council had demolished the houses of more than 20 families in the Mufuchani settlement, saying their plots had been acquired illegally, and that the families were given offer letters for other plots across the Kafue River and put up at a hotel; the report does not connect those demolitions to the bridge resettlement.
